Chapter 6: The Cost of Bearing Witness
There’s a certain weight that comes with seeing what most people turn away from. For Sandra, trauma cleaning was never just about scrubbing floors or tossing out old belongings—it was about carrying the stories, the grief, and the loneliness that clung to every space she entered. Over time, the burden got heavier, and the line between her own pain and what she witnessed started to blur.
Some days, the exhaustion was all physical. The team would wrap up a job, bodies aching, clothes drenched in sweat, the air thick with the sting of bleach and the heaviness of memory. But honestly, the deeper fatigue was always emotional. After clearing out what was left of a life lost to addiction or struggle, Sandra would sometimes just sit in her van, hands trembling, her mind replaying the faces and voices of the ones left behind.
It became impossible to ignore—bearing witness to suffering leaves its mark. It’s a different kind of trauma, one that creeps up quietly.
There were times when the work felt simply overwhelming. One winter, after a string of especially tough jobs, Sandra started to pull away from friends. The sadness was hard to shake. She noticed how easy it was to drift into numbness, how tempting it was to just shut down and stop feeling anything at all. But deep down, she knew—if she let herself go numb, she’d lose the thing that made her truly good at this work: her empathy.
And it wasn’t just Sandra who felt the strain. The whole team was affected. One coworker, usually full of jokes, started snapping over little things, his patience worn thin by the endless cycle of cleaning up after heartbreak. Another began missing shifts, unable to face another day surrounded by loss. Sandra recognized the signs—she’d seen them in herself before. So, she started talking more openly about the toll this job takes. She encouraged her team to speak up, to look out for each other, to share what they were feeling.
It became clear that self-care wasn’t just a nice idea—it was essential. Sandra learned to set boundaries, to step away when she needed a break, and to reach out for support from people who truly understood. She found comfort in small rituals—a hot cup of tea after a brutal day, a quiet walk through the park, the steady presence of her dog curled up beside her. Those little moments became lifelines, gentle reminders that it’s possible to carry the weight without being completely crushed by it.
Most people don’t realize the true cost of this kind of work. Sure, they see the results—a spotless home, a fresh start—but they never see the emotional labor that makes it all possible. For Sandra, the challenge was to keep caring, even when it hurt, to find a way to bear witness without losing herself. It’s a delicate balance, and it needs constant care and attention.
Through everything, Sandra discovered something important. Healing wasn’t just something she offered to others—it was something she had to seek for herself too. Trauma cleaning became a powerful reminder that everyone carries wounds, and that compassion is something we all need, even those who give it most freely.
